clue.text: Morph's dog eating a bone at last

indicators.note: the dog takes the next piece inside it, as if swallowing it

parts.note: a mutt is a mongrel dog

indicators.note: points to the final letter of the word bone

explanation.surface: A plasticine character's pet dog gnawing a bone.
explanation.walkthrough: Morph is a plasticine figure from British children's TV, which makes it look like a name rather than a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Both verbs mean to change form or turn into something different.

clue.text: Earl's determined rent for foreigner

indicators.note: rent is the past tense of rend, torn apart, so the letters are pulled into a new order

explanation.surface: An aristocrat decides on a rent to charge an outsider.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rent' reads as money paid to a landlord but is the past of rend, torn, signalling the anagram.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone from the Arab world or Iran is a foreigner from a British point of view; a specific example of the general word.

clue.text: French love figure that's not fully clothed

parts.note: a figure is a number, here ten

indicators.note: the word for clothed loses its final letter, so it is not complete

parts.note: clothed means dressed

explanation.surface: A sketch or statue of a lover who is only partly dressed.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is borrowed from French for tenderness or fond affection, a kind of love.

clue.text: Idiot's succeeded in unexpected development

indicators.note: the abbreviation for succeeded goes inside the word for idiot

parts.note: a twit is a foolish person
S is the standard abbreviation for succeeded in family trees and lists of rulers

explanation.surface: A fool has unexpectedly done well, which is a surprise.
explanation.definitionFit: A plot turn or surprising development in a story is called this.

clue.text: Soap's so huge (featuring one unpleasant character)

indicators.note: the word for huge has the other pieces included within it

parts.note: epic means on a vast scale
I is the Roman numeral for one
sod is British slang for a nasty person

explanation.surface: A TV soap is so enormous because it includes one horrible villain.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Soap's so' as 'a soap is so': a soap opera is told in instalments.
explanation.definitionFit: A soap opera unfolds in separate instalments, so it has that quality of coming in parts.

clue.text: Some say a morning irritant for fellows

indicators.note: signals that the word is heard as spoken by some people rather than spelt

parts.note: Piers Morgan, the abrasive British presenter of breakfast TV show Good Morning Britain

explanation.surface: People say something annoys them every morning.
explanation.walkthrough: Piers Morgan is a British TV presenter known for provoking viewers on the breakfast programme Good Morning Britain.
explanation.definitionFit: Equals or contemporaries are one's fellows, as in judged by a jury of one's equals.

clue.text: Kelvin, as he was in lumber: 'Get out of here!'

indicators.note: the abbreviations are placed inside the word for lumber

parts.note: to lumber someone with a task is to saddle them with it
K is the symbol for the kelvin, the unit of temperature
Kelvin MacKenzie was editor of The Sun newspaper, and ED is short for editor

explanation.surface: A man named Kelvin, stuck with timber, shouts at someone to go away.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Kelvin' is used twice: as the unit K, and as Kelvin MacKenzie, former editor of The Sun.
explanation.definitionFit: The informal command means scram or clear off, an exclamation telling someone to leave.

clue.text: I'm annoyed about following plan

indicators.note: the exclamation surrounds the abbreviation

parts.note: drat is an exclamation of irritation
F is the abbreviation for following, as in page references

explanation.surface: Someone is irritated about having to follow a scheme.
explanation.definitionFit: A rough first version of a document or scheme is an outline or preliminary plan.

clue.text: Involved in nothing illegal? Breaking the law in nearly all cases!

indicators.note: the words are broken up and their letters rearranged
the word all loses one of its letters, so it is almost complete

explanation.surface: Someone claims they broke no rules, though they broke the law in almost every case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Breaking' sits naturally beside 'the law' but is the anagram signal; 'nearly' trims ALL to AL before the shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means entirely innocent or free of any wrongdoing.

clue.text: Riddle of back-to-front shoes

indicators.note: the final letter of the shoe word moves from the back to the front

parts.note: trainers are sports shoes

explanation.surface: A puzzle about shoes worn the wrong way round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Riddle' looks like a puzzle but here is a coarse sieve; as a verb, to riddle is to sift.
explanation.definitionFit: A riddle is a large sieve, a device for sifting soil or gravel.

clue.text: He's indecent! Name unholy terror who's stripped

indicators.note: something unholy is wicked or disordered, so the letters are thrown into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: An outraged cry demanding the name of an indecent streaker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stripped' suggests undressing but means appearing in a comic strip, here The Beano.
explanation.definitionFit: The Beano comic's mischievous boy is a little terror who appears in comic strips.

clue.text: Learning to race with a female

parts.note: lore is traditional knowledge or learning
the TT is the Tourist Trophy motorcycle race on the Isle of Man

explanation.surface: Studying how to race alongside a woman.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a woman's given name, so it names a female.

clue.text: Quarrel about rule with an ascetic

indicators.note: the quarrel word goes around the abbreviation

parts.note: a spat is a petty quarrel

explanation.surface: An argument over regulations with a self-denying hermit.
explanation.definitionFit: Austere and self-denying, like the frugal citizens of ancient Sparta.

clue.text: Take in lustre in object regarded as sacred

indicators.note: the combined piece then goes inside the word for object

parts.note: an end is an aim or object

indicators.note: the letter for take goes inside the word for lustre

parts.note: shine is a gleam or lustre
R is the abbreviation for recipe, Latin for take, written on prescriptions

explanation.surface: Absorbing the gleam of an object treated as holy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take in' reads as one phrase but splits: 'Take' is R and 'in' places it.
explanation.definitionFit: Something cherished and preserved as if in a holy casket is held sacred.

clue.text: Relaxed about exercise, Charlie appreciated

indicators.note: the word for relaxed goes around the other pieces

parts.note: rested means relaxed
PE is physical education
C is Charlie in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: Someone at ease with fitness work valued a friend named Charlie.
explanation.definitionFit: To be held in esteem and valued is to be thought highly of.

clue.text: Point at exotic tree with large bird

parts.note: a dot is a point

indicators.note: exotic suggests something strange and foreign, so the letters are altered

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for large on clothing labels

explanation.surface: Pointing at a foreign tree where a big bird is perched.
explanation.definitionFit: The dotterel is a kind of plover, a wading bird.

clue.text: Perverse — boss's son in detention daily does this

indicators.note: per verse, read as in reverse, so the letters run backwards
the son is held inside the word for boss

parts.note: a stud is a boss, a knob projecting from a surface

explanation.surface: A perverse boss keeps his son in detention every day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'daily' is a British cleaning lady, not 'every day'; 'boss' is a stud, not an employer.
explanation.definitionFit: A daily is a cleaner, who removes the dust from furniture as part of her work.

clue.text: Sister annoyed with singer

indicators.note: annoyed suggests being stirred up, so the letters are shuffled

parts.note: and means with or together with

explanation.surface: A nun is irritated by a vocalist.
explanation.definitionFit: Barbra is a famous American singer and actress.

clue.text: The Kardashians maybe busy — bless!

indicators.note: busy suggests bustling activity, so the letters move around

explanation.surface: The Kardashian family are always busy, bless them.
explanation.definitionFit: The Kardashians are an example of celebrities, for which the slang is a clipped form.

clue.text: Tired rider edges out round bridle path in capital

indicators.note: turns the whole string backwards, as when something comes round

parts.note: worn means tired out

indicators.note: the jockey's name loses its first and last letters

parts.note: Frankie Dettori is a famous jockey

explanation.surface: An exhausted jockey narrowly beats rivals on a lap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'edges out' looks like winning narrowly but means dropping the rider's outer letters; 'round' then turns everything backwards. Frankie Dettori is a celebrated Italian-born jockey in British racing.
explanation.definitionFit: This sandy track along Hyde Park in London is a historic place for horse riding, a bridleway in the capital.

clue.text: Plain paper

definitions.meaning: clear and explicit, as in an explicit instruction
the Daily ..., a British national newspaper

explanation.surface: A plain newspaper.
explanation.definitionFit: An explicit wish is plainly stated; the Daily Express is a British tabloid newspaper.

clue.text: Image production trouble for gallery

parts.note: PR, public relations, is the business of producing an image
ado means fuss or trouble

explanation.surface: Problems in making pictures for an art gallery.
explanation.definitionFit: The Prado is the national art museum in Madrid.

clue.text: Hunt through — and bitter about Cameron's leadership

indicators.note: the word for bitter goes around the initial

parts.note: sour means bitter

indicators.note: the leading letter of the name Cameron

explanation.surface: Bitter feelings about David Cameron's time as party leader.
explanation.walkthrough: David Cameron was the UK's Conservative prime minister when this appeared.
explanation.definitionFit: To search a place thoroughly is to comb or hunt through it.

clue.text: 'This writer is boring' — I object, backing old academics

indicators.note: the whole string is read backwards

parts.note: the setter refers to themself as I
to tire is to bore
me is the object form of the pronoun I

explanation.surface: Someone protests at being called dull, while supporting retired professors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I object' looks like a protest but is grammar: the objective case of I.
explanation.definitionFit: Retired professors who keep their title honorifically; this is the Latin plural.

clue.text: Racecourse town in Wales he remembered

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: He recalled a town with a racecourse in Wales.
explanation.walkthrough: Wales is a red herring: the town is in Surrey, England, home of Sandown Park racecourse.
explanation.definitionFit: Sandown Park racecourse is in this Surrey town, so it is a racecourse town.

clue.text: The reason ornate building is loved

definitions.note: a verb phrase, matched by the phrase meaning dear to someone

indicators.note: building means assembling the letters into a new structure

explanation.surface: Explaining why a fancy building is so cherished.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes something held dear, deeply cherished by a person.

clue.text: Further requests from registrars — no contracts first and foremost

indicators.note: says the following letter is absent from the word for registrars

parts.note: recorders are officials who keep records, as registrars do

indicators.note: takes the leading letter of the word contracts

explanation.surface: Officials make more demands, with no contracts at the top of the list.
explanation.definitionFit: Placing fresh orders for goods are further requests for supply.

clue.text: Plod right to detain BBC man

indicators.note: the word for right holds the abbreviation inside it

parts.note: true means correct or right
the DG, Director-General, is the head of the BBC

explanation.surface: A police officer, a plod, is right to arrest a BBC man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Plod' looks like British slang for the police but is the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To walk heavily and wearily is to plod.
